title: POC acceptance matrix + TTFT/TPOT edge-cases workshop
summary: Workshop to agree on POC acceptance matrix for latency SLOs (TTFT vs TPOT), define p95/p99 targets across traffic slices, and outline measurement plan and timelines. Emphasis on tail behavior for long prompts, bursty traffic, and failure/fallback policies.
topics: Clarify TTFT vs TPOT definitions and measurement boundaries
Set p95/p99 targets across short/medium/long prompt buckets
Traffic shaping and QPS/burst sizing for pilot
Benchmark methodology, sampling cadence, and artifacts to collect
Rollout timeline, canary percentages, and success criteria
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. We want to walk through the acceptance matrix for the POC, specifically how we measure TTFT versus TPOT and what counts as pass/fail.
[00:12] Lena Ortiz: Thanks Maya. Quick context — we run a mixture of short symptom queries and longer clinical-note summarizations, so latency is critical on the short ones but we also see long tail on the long ones.
[00:27] Ethan Park: Got it. For clarity, when we say TTFT we mean "time to first token" measured from request arrival at the model control plane to emission of the first token. TPOT we use as "time per token" or total per-token throughput — sometimes customers call it per-token-latency or tokens/sec equivalent.
[00:43] Marcus Vale: Quick interjection, we've seen different vendors measure TTFT differently — some exclude network time inside the infra. We need a strict definition.
[00:50] Maya Chen: Agree. Proposal: TTFT measured at Redwood edge (post-ingress) to first token out of the inference runtime; include queuing inside the dedicated GPU pool but exclude client-side retry/backoff. We'll record both edge-to-edge and model-runtime-only numbers.
[01:05] Priya Nair: So we'll get two metrics — observed TTFT and runtime TTFT — useful for isolating networking vs scheduling. Good.
[01:12] Ethan Park: For TPOT we'll report median token time and p95/p99 of per-token emission, plus aggregate tokens/sec under sustained load. We'll also measure total request completion time for long responses (e.g., 1024-token summaries).
[01:27] Tomás Ruiz: How do we bucket prompts?
[01:30] Maya Chen: Recommended buckets: short (<=16 tokens), medium (17-128 tokens), long (129-1024 tokens). We'll capture sample sizes per bucket. For Helicon's workload Marcus said 60% short, 30% medium, 10% long as an estimate.
[01:44] Marcus Vale: Correct, that's current traffic pattern. Peak QPS during business hours hits ~250 but can burst to 800 during batch ingest windows.
[01:52] Ethan Park: Ok we'll plan benchmarks at baseline QPS 250 sustained, burst tests to 800 for 2-5 minute intervals, and long-run sustained tests for 30 minutes to evaluate thermal behavior.
[02:05] Lena Ortiz: SLO targets — what are we thinking p95/p99?
[02:08] Maya Chen: Initial proposal from Redwood: TTFT p95 <= 150ms for short, p99 <= 350ms; medium TTFT p95 <= 200ms p99 <= 500ms; long TTFT p95 <= 350ms p99 <= 900ms. TPOT (per-token) p95 <= 40ms p99 <= 90ms for steady emission. For total completion on 1024-token jobs we propose p95 <= 40s p99 <= 70s as a checkpoint. These are starting points, open to negotiation.
[02:35] Marcus Vale: The p99 for long seems optimistic but OK as a target if we get caching and batching. Need to document fallbacks if we miss SLOs.
[02:44] Ethan Park: We'll include fallback playbook: automatic model-variant fallback (quantized model), region failover, and graceful degradation to partial responses with a retry header. We'll test each fallback path in the POC.
[02:57] Tomás Ruiz: Measurement plan detail — sampling, instrumentation, and artifacts?
[03:01] Maya Chen: We'll instrument at three points: client SDK, Redwood edge, and runtime. For each request we'll capture timestamps, request size, token counts, model variant, queue depth, and kernel/quantization config. Benchmark sessions will be run with fixed seed prompts and a synthetic traffic generator that replays Helicon's traffic mix.
[03:19] Priya Nair: We also need percentile histograms and raw traces for p99 debug — sample the full request/response for 1% of traffic and collect full cdrs for failing requests.
[03:29] Ethan Park: Agreed. We'll provide pre-built Grafana dashboards and a shared BigQuery sheet with raw samples. We'll also provide a reproducible benchmark harness (JAR + scripts) that you can run in your staging VPC or we can run from Redwood Dedicated environment.
[03:45] Lena Ortiz: Which environment will we use for initial runs? We prefer dedicated but can start hosted if it's faster.
[03:50] Maya Chen: For the POC we recommend Redwood Dedicated (reserved GPU pool) to match production isolation and queuing behavior. If you want quick numbers we can run a hosted baseline first.
[03:59] Marcus Vale: Dedicated is preferred. Can you size the pilot? GPU counts, expected capacity?
[04:04] Ethan Park: Based on your traffic and the model (we'll be using an open LLM ~7B quantized) initial sizing for sustained 250 QPS with low-latency targets suggests 4 GPU nodes with continuous batching; burst headroom to 8 nodes with autoscale. We'll run tuning iterations to potentially reduce to 3 nodes after optimizations. We'll include a conservative CPU/memory sizing for pre and post-processing.
[04:24] Tomás Ruiz: Can you put that in the acceptance matrix?
[04:27] Maya Chen: Yes — acceptance matrix will list traffic slice, SLOs (TTFT/TPOT p95/p99), sampling plan, and pass criteria: 7/10 test windows must meet p95 and 9/10 must meet p99 for short/medium buckets, long bucket slightly looser 6/10 for p95 and 8/10 for p99. We debated thresholds; feel free to push back.
[04:46] Marcus Vale: Those pass ratios look workable. We also require that no single outage >5 minutes occurs during the 2-week acceptance window.
[04:53] Maya Chen: Noted — we'll include uptime/incident criteria.
[04:57] Ethan Park: Edge cases: cold start vs hot path. We'll capture cold-start TTFT by cycling containers and measuring restart behavior; cold starts must be documented but won't count against acceptance if they occur during deployment windows only.
[05:12] Priya Nair: Important: We need to validate telemetry integrity and SSO for metric export to our monitoring. We'll need an export hook and role-based access for dashboards.
[05:20] Maya Chen: We'll share a telemetry integration guide (Prometheus/Grafana exporter and BigQuery sink) and set up read-only dashboards for Helicon.
[05:27] Tomás Ruiz: Timeline?
[05:29] Maya Chen: Proposed timeline: Week 0 (this week) - kickoff and infra provisioning; Week 1 - baseline runs and short smoke benchmarks; Week 2 - tuning and quantization testing; Week 3 - acceptance window (running multiple windows, including burst tests); Week 4 - wrap and decision. Total ~4 weeks. We can compress to 3 weeks if you can provide staging VPC and creds quickly.
[05:50] Lena Ortiz: We'll try for the 3-week cadence. Who owns the benchmark harness run?
[05:54] Ethan Park: Redwood SE will run initial harness in Redwood Dedicated, then hand you the harness and infra-as-code to run inside your staging VPC. We'll train a Helicon infra engineer on day 3.
[06:03] Marcus Vale: Concerning data residency and logs, we need logs retained for 90 days in our tenancy and KMS keys for any sensitive payloads.
[06:11] Maya Chen: We support customer-managed KMS and log export. We'll add that requirement to the POC scope and include SOC2/ISO references.
[06:18] Tomás Ruiz: Any competitor comparisons to call out?
[06:21] Maya Chen: You mentioned before looking at Anthropic and a self-hosted stack on SageMaker. We'll note comparative test coverage but not run direct vendor-to-vendor tests unless you request.
[06:31] Lena Ortiz: Ok. Final recap please.
[06:33] Maya Chen: Recap: agree on strict TTFT/TPOT definitions; buckets short/medium/long; SLO targets (we'll share the spreadsheet with exact numbers); sampling plan with 1% deep traces; benchmark harness + dashboards; Dedicated environment with initial 4 GPUs and autoscale to 8 for bursts; timeline ~3-4 weeks; acceptance matrix pass ratios and uptime criteria; fallbacks to quantized model and regional failover tested.
[06:56] Marcus Vale: Sounds good. A couple action items and we'll schedule kickoff.
[06:59] Tomás Ruiz: Thanks everyone.
